Where this chapter sits in the course
Chapter 1 gives the toolkit for everything that follows: waveguides and fibers (Ch. 2), LEDs and semiconductor optics (Ch. 3), lasers and amplifiers (Ch. 4), photodetectors (Ch. 5), and polarisation and modulation (Ch. 6). WarningSign convention (read this once)



The slides (following Kasap) use the engineering convention \(E\propto\exp[j(\omega t-kz)]\), which gives a complex index \(N=n-jK\) and a relative permittivity \(\varepsilon_r=\varepsilon_r'-j\varepsilon_r''\). Most physics texts (Born & Wolf, Saleh & Teich, Jackson) use \(\exp[i(kz-\omega t)]\) and \(N=n+i\kappa\). All code here follows the slide convention. Whenever you consult another book, check the convention first: most “wrong sign” errors in Fresnel phases, evanescent fields and Kramers–Kronig relations come from mixing the two.

title: 1  Electromagnetic waves
text:
1.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 11–24: Maxwell’s equations, the spectrum, plane waves, phase velocity, phase change, exponential notation, wave vector, spherical waves, divergence.
Light is a travelling electromagnetic wave whose electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation (slide 13). The simplest solution of Maxwell’s wave equation is the monochromatic plane wave (slides 14–15):
\[
E_x(z,t)=E_0\cos(\omega t-kz+\phi_0),\qquad k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda},\quad \omega=2\pi\nu,\quad
v=\frac{\omega}{k}=\nu\lambda,\quad \Delta\phi=k\,\Delta z .
\]

1.3 Worked example: phase is what we engineer in integrated photonics
The phase difference \(\Delta\phi=k\,\Delta z\) (slide 19) is the quantity that every phase shifter, interferometric modulator or optical switch manipulates. In a silicon waveguide with a thermo-optic coefficient \(dn/dT\approx1.8\times10^{-4}\) K⁻¹ (typical value for Si near 1550 nm), a heater of length \(L\) produces \(\Delta\phi=(2\pi/\lambda)(dn/dT)\,\Delta T\,L\).


Show the Python
dndT = 1.8e-4          # K^-1, typical Si value (bulk value, confinement ≈ 1)
for L in (um(50), um(100), um(500)):
    print(f"L = {L*1e6:5.0f} µm  ->  ΔT for a π shift = {nm(1550)/(2*dndT*L):5.1f} K")


L =    50 µm  ->  ΔT for a π shift =  86.1 K
L =   100 µm  ->  ΔT for a π shift =  43.1 K
L =   500 µm  ->  ΔT for a π shift =   8.6 K


The same calculation, with an electro-optic or plasma-dispersion \(\Delta n\) instead of the thermo-optic one, is the core of Chapter 6 (light modulation).

title: 1  Electromagnetic waves
text:
1.4 Plane waves build every beam (slides 22–24)
A plane wave is unphysical (infinite extent), but because the wave equation is linear, any field can be written as a superposition of plane waves. Summing plane waves with a spread of transverse wave vectors \(k_x\) produces a localised, focused beam. The angular spread of the wave vectors is the divergence (slide 24).


Show the Python
lam = 1.0; k = 2*np.pi/lam
x = np.linspace(-15, 15, 400); z = np.linspace(0, 30, 400)
X, Z = np.meshgrid(x, z)
single = np.cos(k*Z)
kx = np.linspace(-0.8*k, 0.8*k, 81)
wts = np.exp(-(kx/(0.35*k))**2)
beam = sum(w*np.cos(kxi*X + np.sqrt(k**2 - kxi**2)*(Z - 15)) for w, kxi in zip(wts, kx))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.8), sharey=True)
for a, f, t in zip(ax, (single, beam), ("plane wave", "superposition of plane waves")):
    a.imshow(f, extent=[x[0], x[-1], z[0], z[-1]], origin="lower", cmap="RdBu", aspect="auto")
    a.set_title(t); a.set_xlabel("x / λ"); a.grid(False)
ax[0].set_ylabel("z / λ"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Figure 1.1: Left: a single plane wave. Right: 81 plane waves with Gaussian-weighted transverse wave vectors build a beam focused at z = 15λ (instantaneous field, t = 0).











TipGoing deeper






Derive \(\nabla^2\mathbf E=\mu\varepsilon\,\partial_t^2\mathbf E\) from the curl equations, and identify where the assumptions “no free charge”, “linear”, “isotropic” and “homogeneous” enter. Which assumption fails first in a waveguide? (Answer in Chapter 2.)
Show that for a plane wave \(|\mathbf B|=|\mathbf E|/v\), and estimate the ratio of magnetic to electric force on a bound electron. This justifies why “optical field” means \(\mathbf E\) (slide 16).
The superposition above is the angular spectrum representation. It reappears as the Fraunhofer–Fourier link in Chapter 13 and as the modal expansion in waveguides.
Why does the spherical-wave amplitude decay as \(1/r\) (slide 23)? Relate it to energy conservation through spheres of increasing radius (Chapter 3).
Scalar versus vector optics: when does treating \(E_x\) as a scalar fail? (High-NA focusing, sub-wavelength waveguides.)

title: 2  Gaussian beams
text:
2.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 25–34 and 79–84: intensity profile, Rayleigh range, divergence, \(M^2\), Gaussian beam in a cavity, power and irradiance of a Gaussian beam.
The output of most lasers, and the fundamental mode of a single-mode fiber (slide 27), is a Gaussian beam. Its irradiance across the beam is Gaussian (slides 26, 80):
\[
I(r,z)=\frac{2P}{\pi w^2(z)}\exp\!\left(-\frac{2r^2}{w^2(z)}\right),\qquad
w(z)=w_0\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{z}{z_0}\right)^2},\qquad z_0=\frac{\pi w_0^2 n}{\lambda}.
\]
The complex beam parameter \(q(z)=z+jz_0\) (engineering convention: \(1/q=1/R-j\lambda/(\pi w^2)\)) packs \(w\) and \(R\) into one number. It transforms through any paraxial optical system with its \(ABCD\) matrix: \(q'=(Aq+B)/(Cq+D)\).

The same formulas size the transmitter of a LiDAR: how large must the output waist be to keep a small footprint at 100 m?

fig, ax = plt.subplots()

ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=2); plt.show()
for zt in (50, 100, 200):
    print(f"optimum waist for range {zt} m: w0 = √(λz/π) = {np.sqrt(nm(905)*zt/np.pi)*1e3:.2f} mm")








Figure 2.1: Spot diameter of a 905 nm LiDAR beam versus distance for three output waists, with ideal (M² = 1, solid) and real (M² = 1.5, dashed) beams. A small waist diverges fast; a large waist stays large.





optimum waist for range 50 m: w0 = √(λz/π) = 3.80 mm
optimum waist for range 100 m: w0 = √(λz/π) = 5.37 mm

The optimum waist for a given range \(z\) minimises \(w(z)\): \(w_0^\text{opt}=\sqrt{\lambda z/\pi}\), that is \(z=z_0\).

section: 2.4 Worked example: focusing into a single-mode fiber
text:
2.4 Worked example: focusing into a single-mode fiber
A common laboratory task: couple a collimated 1550 nm beam into an SMF-28 fiber (mode-field diameter ≈ 10.4 µm, so \(w_f\approx5.2\) µm). The fiber mode is well approximated by a Gaussian (slide 27), so the power coupling efficiency between two Gaussians with waists \(w_1, w_2\) and lateral offset \(d\) at a common waist plane is
\[
\eta=\left(\frac{2w_1w_2}{w_1^2+w_2^2}\right)^2\exp\!\left(-\frac{2d^2}{w_1^2+w_2^2}\right).
\]


Show the Python
lam, wf, w_in = nm(1550), um(5.2), 1.0e-3
f = np.linspace(2e-3, 20e-3, 300)
w_focus = []
for fi in f:
    q = ol.abcd(ol.q_from_w0(w_in, lam), ol.lens(fi))     # just after the lens
    w_focus.append(ol.w_from_q(ol.abcd(q, ol.free(-np.real(q))), lam))   # new waist where Re(q) = 0
w_focus = np.array(w_focus)
eta = (2*w_focus*wf/(w_focus**2 + wf**2))**2
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
ax[0].plot(f*1e3, 100*eta)
f_opt = np.pi*w_in*wf/lam
ax[0].axvline(f_opt*1e3, ls=":", c=ol.INK2)
ax[0].text(f_opt*1e3 + 0.3, 20, f"f = πw·w_f/λ = {f_opt*1e3:.1f} mm", color=ol.INK2)
ax[0].set(xlabel="lens focal length (mm)", ylabel="η (%)", title="mode matching")
d = np.linspace(0, 8e-6, 200)
ax[1].plot(d*1e6, -ol.dB(np.exp(-2*d**2/(2*wf**2))))
ax[1].set(xlabel="lateral offset (µm)", ylabel="excess loss (dB)", title="alignment tolerance")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Figure 2.2: Left: coupling efficiency into SMF-28 versus the focal length of the coupling lens (1 mm input beam radius). Right: excess loss versus lateral misalignment for perfectly matched waists.





An offset of 1.5 µm already costs about 0.35 dB. This is why fiber-to-chip packaging is a precision-mechanics problem, and why silicon photonic chips use spot-size converters (inverse tapers) or grating couplers to enlarge their ~0.5 µm mode.

title: 2  Gaussian beams
text:
2.5 Gaussian beam in a cavity (slide 32)
Between two spherical mirrors, the Gaussian beam is a self-consistent solution: the wavefront curvature \(R(z)\) matches the mirror curvature at both ends. For a symmetric confocal cavity (\(R_\text{mirror}=L\)), the waist is \(w_0=\sqrt{\lambda L/2\pi}\).


Show the Python
L, lam = 0.30, nm(633)
w0 = np.sqrt(lam*L/(2*np.pi)); z0 = np.pi*w0**2/lam
z = np.linspace(-L/2, L/2, 400)
w = w0*np.sqrt(1 + (z/z0)**2)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
ax.fill_between(z*100, -w*1e3, w*1e3, color=ol.PALETTE[0], alpha=0.25, lw=0)
ax.plot(z*100, w*1e3, color=ol.PALETTE[0]); ax.plot(z*100, -w*1e3, color=ol.PALETTE[0])
yy = np.linspace(-1.6*w.max()*1e3, 1.6*w.max()*1e3, 50)
for zm, s in ((L/2, 1), (-L/2, -1)):
    ax.plot((zm - s*(L - np.sqrt(L**2 - (yy*1e-3)**2)))*100, yy, color=ol.PALETTE[1], lw=3)
ax.set(xlabel="z (cm)", ylabel="w (mm)", title=f"confocal cavity: w₀ = {w0*1e3:.3f} mm, z₀ = L/2 = {z0*100:.1f} cm")
plt.show()








Figure 2.3: Gaussian beam inside a symmetric confocal cavity (L = 30 cm, 633 nm). The mirrors (orange) sit where the wavefront radius equals the mirror radius.

TipGoing deeper






Why is the “86 % power” diameter \(2w\) (slide 82)? Integrate the Gaussian and show that the fraction inside \(r=w\) is \(1-e^{-2}\).
The Gouy phase \(\psi(z)\) is missing from the slide formulas. It shifts the resonance frequencies of transverse modes in a spherical-mirror cavity (slide 32): \(\nu_{mnq}=\frac{c}{2nL}\left[q+(m+n+1)\frac{\Delta\psi}{\pi}\right]\). Look up Hermite–Gaussian modes and explain why a confocal cavity is degenerate.
\(M^2\) can be defined from second moments of the intensity (ISO 11146). Why do the second moments fail for a top-hat beam with hard edges (sinc² far field)?
The beam parameter product \(w_0\theta=M^2\lambda/\pi\) is invariant through lossless optics (étendue). Relate it to the brightness theorem and to why an LED cannot be focused into a single-mode fiber efficiently (Chapter 3).
Fiber modes are only approximately Gaussian. The Marcuse formula \(w/a\approx0.65+1.619V^{-3/2}+2.879V^{-6}\) links \(w\) to the normalised frequency \(V\) of Chapter 2.

title: 3  Irradiance and the Poynting vector
text:
3.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 70–84: magnetic field of the wave, energy density, Poynting vector, average irradiance, spherical waves, power in a Gaussian beam.
The magnetic field always accompanies the electric field, with \(B_y=E_x/v\) and \(v=c/n\) (slide 71). The energy densities of the two fields are equal, so the total energy density is \(\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_rE_x^2\) (slide 73). Energy flows along \(\mathbf k\) with the Poynting vector (slides 74–75):
\[
\mathbf S=v^2\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r\,\mathbf E\times\mathbf B,\qquad
I=\langle S\rangle=\tfrac12 v\,\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_rE_0^2=\tfrac12 c\,\varepsilon_0nE_0^2 .
\]
The deep-dive chapter Chapter 15 derives Poynting’s theorem step by step and answers the classic objection: how can energy flow through vacuum, where there is no current?

title: 5  Group velocity and group index
text:
5.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 60–69: wave packets, beat of two waves, group velocity \(v_g=d\omega/dk\), group index \(N_g=n-\lambda\,dn/d\lambda\).
There are no perfectly monochromatic waves (slide 60). Two waves at \(\omega\pm\delta\omega\) with wave vectors \(k\pm\delta k\) add up to (slides 64–65)
\[
E_x=2E_0\cos(\delta\omega\,t-\delta k\,z)\cos(\omega t-kz),
\]
a carrier at \(\omega\) modulated by a slow envelope. The envelope, which carries energy and information, travels at the group velocity (slides 61, 66–68):
\[
v_g=\frac{d\omega}{dk}=\frac{c}{N_g},\qquad N_g=n-\lambda\frac{dn}{d\lambda}.
\]
In a dispersive medium (\(n\) depends on \(\lambda\)), \(v_g\neq v\). For silica in the near IR, \(N_g\approx1.46\) while \(n\approx1.44\) (slide 69).

text:
6.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 85–100 (Snell–Descartes law from phase matching, critical angle, total internal reflection, prisms, lateral displacement, light guiding in fibers and water jets) and slides 296–299 (Fermat’s principle).
At a boundary, the incident, reflected and transmitted waves must stay in phase along the interface. This gives \(\theta_r=\theta_i\) (slide 88) and, because the wavefront travels \(v_1\Delta t\) in medium 1 while it travels \(v_2\Delta t\) in medium 2, Snell’s law (slides 89–90):
\[
n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t ,\qquad \sin\theta_c=\frac{n_2}{n_1}\quad(n_1>n_2).
\]
Beyond the critical angle there is no transmitted wave: total internal reflection (TIR, slides 91–93), with an evanescent field in medium 2 (Chapter 7). Snell’s law is equivalent to conservation of the tangential wave vector, \(k_1\sin\theta_i=k_2\sin\theta_t\).

title: 7  Fresnel equations, Brewster angle and evanescent waves
text:
7.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 101–147: polarised light, boundary conditions, \(r_\perp,r_\parallel,t_\perp,t_\parallel\), internal and external reflection, Brewster angle, phase change on TIR, evanescent wave, Goos–Hänchen shift, frustrated TIR and beam-splitter cubes, reflectance and transmittance.
Resolve the field into components perpendicular (\(\perp\), TE) and parallel (\(\parallel\), TM) to the plane of incidence (slide 103). The boundary conditions (continuity of tangential \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\), slides 106–108) give, with \(n=n_2/n_1\), Fresnel’s equations (slides 110–111):
\[
r_\perp=\frac{\cos\theta_i-\sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta_i}}{\cos\theta_i+\sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta_i}},\qquad
r_\parallel=\frac{\sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta_i}-n^2\cos\theta_i}{\sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta_i}+n^2\cos\theta_i},
\] \[
t_\perp=\frac{2\cos\theta_i}{\cos\theta_i+\sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta_i}},\qquad
t_\parallel=\frac{2n\cos\theta_i}{n^2\cos\theta_i+\sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta_i}},\qquad
r_\parallel+nt_\parallel=1,\quad r_\perp+1=t_\perp .
\]
The square root \(\sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta_i}\) is taken on the branch with non-positive imaginary part. That is the physical choice in the \(e^{j\omega t}\) convention, where the transmitted field decays into medium 2 under TIR. With this choice ol.fresnel reproduces the slide phases.

Show the Python

ax.plot(y[y >= 0]*1e6, E2[y >= 0], label="medium 2 (evanescent)")
ax.set(xlabel="distance from interface y (µm)", ylabel="|E⊥| (a.u.)"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)

Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).

A perfect sine wave is perfectly coherent and has a single frequency. A finite wave train of duration \(\Delta t\) has a spectrum of width \(\Delta\nu\approx1/\Delta t\) (slides 164–167). Two parts of a beam can only interfere if their path difference is shorter than the coherence length:
\[
\Delta t\approx\frac{1}{\Delta\nu},\qquad l_c=c\,\Delta t=\frac{c}{\Delta\nu}=\frac{\lambda^2}{\Delta\lambda}.
\]

title: 10  Interference and interferometers
text:
Constructive interference: \(I_\text{max}=I_1+I_2+2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\), which is \(4I_1\) for equal beams.
Destructive interference: \(I_\text{min}=I_1+I_2-2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\), which is \(0\) for equal beams.
Incoherent waves simply add their intensities, \(I=I_1+I_2\) (slide 174).
Fringe visibility \(V=(I_\text{max}-I_\text{min})/(I_\text{max}+I_\text{min})=2\sqrt{I_1I_2}/(I_1+I_2)\).

10.3 Worked example: the Mach–Zehnder as modulator and as wavelength filter

text:
11.4 The photonic band gap behind the Bragg mirror (slides 289–294)
For an infinite bilayer lattice of period \(\Lambda=d_1+d_2\), Bloch’s theorem gives the dispersion relation of the 1D photonic crystal (slide 292):
\[
\cos(K\Lambda)=\cos(k_1d_1)\cos(k_2d_2)-\tfrac12\left(\tfrac{n_1}{n_2}+\tfrac{n_2}{n_1}\right)\sin(k_1d_1)\sin(k_2d_2).
\]
Where the right-hand side exceeds 1 in magnitude, \(K\) is complex: no propagating Bloch wave exists, and a finite stack reflects.


Show the Python
n1, n2, Lam = 2.49, 1.55, 1.0
d1, d2 = Lam*n2/(n1 + n2), Lam*n1/(n1 + n2)     # quarter-wave condition n1 d1 = n2 d2
f = np.linspace(1e-3, 1.0, 3000)                 # normalised frequency Λ/λ
k0 = 2*np.pi*f/Lam
rhs = np.cos(k0*n1*d1)*np.cos(k0*n2*d2) - 0.5*(n1/n2 + n2/n1)*np.sin(k0*n1*d1)*np.sin(k0*n2*d2)
gap = np.abs(rhs) > 1
KL = np.where(gap, np.nan, np.arccos(np.clip(rhs, -1, 1))/np.pi)
R8 = ol.tmm([1.0] + [n1, n2]*8 + [1.0], [d1, d2]*8, Lam/f)[0]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2), sharey=True)
ax[0].plot(KL, f); ax[0].set(xlabel="Bloch wave vector KΛ/π", ylabel="normalised frequency Λ/λ", xlim=(0, 1))
ax[1].plot(R8, f); ax[1].set(xlabel="R (N = 8)", xlim=(0, 1.05))
idx = np.where(gap)[0]
for blk in np.split(idx, np.where(np.diff(idx) > 1)[0] + 1):
    if blk.size:
        for a in ax: a.axhspan(f[blk[0]], f[blk[-1]], color=ol.PALETTE[3], alpha=0.2, lw=0)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Figure 11.2: Left: band diagram of a TiO₂/SiO₂ quarter-wave 1D photonic crystal. Right: reflectance of an 8-period finite stack on the same frequency axis. The shaded bands are the photonic band gaps.





The stop band of the finite stack coincides with the photonic band gap of the infinite crystal, and the index contrast sets the gap width. The “interference of reflections” picture explains why a band gap appears; the Bloch picture gives its size. In 2D and 3D (slides 289–293), a full band gap needs a large contrast and the right lattice. Point defects then act as cavities and line defects as waveguides (slide 294).

11.5 Worked example: a fiber Bragg grating
A fiber Bragg grating (FBG) is a Bragg mirror with a tiny index contrast (\(\Delta n\sim10^{-4}\)) but tens of thousands of periods. The same transfer-matrix approach applies; Chapter 2 treats FBGs in detail (coupled-mode theory, apodisation, sensing).


Show the Python
def periodic_R(n0, na, nb, da, db, N, ns, lam):
    def layer(n, d):
        dl = 2*np.pi*n*d/lam
        M = np.empty((lam.size, 2, 2), complex)
        M[:, 0, 0] = np.cos(dl); M[:, 0, 1] = 1j*np.sin(dl)/n
        M[:, 1, 0] = 1j*n*np.sin(dl); M[:, 1, 1] = np.cos(dl)
        return M
    M = np.linalg.matrix_power(layer(na, da) @ layer(nb, db), N)
    B = M[:, 0, 0] + M[:, 0, 1]*ns; C = M[:, 1, 0] + M[:, 1, 1]*ns
    return np.abs((n0*B - C)/(n0*B + C))**2

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for dn, Lg in ((1e-4, 5e-3), (1e-4, 20e-3), (5e-4, 10e-3)):
    na, nb = neff, neff + dn
    da, db = lamB/(4*na), lamB/(4*nb)
    N = int(Lg/(da + db))
    ax.plot((lam - lamB)*1e12, periodic_R(neff, na, nb, da, db, N, neff, lam),
            label=f"Δn = {dn:.0e}, L = {Lg*1e3:.0f} mm ({N} periods)")
ax.set(xlabel="λ − λ_B (pm)", ylabel="R"); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show()

title: 12  Optical resonators: the Fabry–Perot cavity
text:
12.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 191–209: cavity modes, free spectral range, finesse, mode linewidth, Q-factor, etalons, scanning Fabry–Perot interferometer, mirror requirements, worked examples.
Two parallel mirrors of reflectance \(R\) separated by \(L\) trap light. The circulating field is the sum of all round trips (slide 194), \(E_\text{cavity}=A+Ar^2e^{-j2kL}+Ar^4e^{-j4kL}+\dots\), which peaks when \(k_mL=m\pi\). The allowed standing waves are the cavity modes (slides 193–196):
\[
m\frac{\lambda_m}{2}=nL,\qquad \nu_m=m\frac{c}{2nL},\qquad \nu_f=\frac{c}{2nL}\ \text{(free spectral range)},
\] \[
\mathcal F=\frac{\pi\sqrt R}{1-R},\qquad \delta\nu_m=\frac{\nu_f}{\mathcal F},\qquad Q=\frac{\nu_m}{\delta\nu_m}=m\mathcal F .
\]
The cavity is also a filter: only its modes are transmitted (slide 198). A lossless cavity has the Airy transmission \(T=\dfrac{(1-R)^2}{(1-R)^2+4R\sin^2(2\pi nL/\lambda)}\). For a finesse above about 100, only multilayer dielectric mirrors (Chapter 11) are good enough (slide 204).

13.6 Worked example: the Arago (Poisson) spot (slides 219–220)
The angular-spectrum method propagates any field by multiplying its 2-D FFT by \(e^{-jk_zz}\), with \(k_z=\sqrt{k^2-k_x^2-k_y^2}\). It is the plane-wave superposition of Chapter 1 made quantitative. A band limit (Matsushima & Shimobaba, 2009) avoids aliasing at long distances.


Show the Python
lam, N, Lw = nm(633), 1024, 12e-3
dx = Lw/N; x = (np.arange(N) - N//2)*dx
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, x); r = np.hypot(X, Y)
a_disk, w_ill = 1e-3, 3e-3
U0 = np.exp(-(r/w_ill)**2)*(r > a_disk)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.8))
for axi, z in zip(ax, (0.05, 0.2, 1.0)):
    I = np.abs(ol.asm_propagate(U0, dx, lam, z))**2
    axi.imshow(I, extent=[x[0]*1e3, x[-1]*1e3]*2, cmap="inferno", vmax=1.0)
    axi.set(title=f"z = {z} m, N_F = {a_disk**2/(lam*z):.1f}", xlabel="x (mm)"); axi.grid(False)
    print(f"z = {z:4.2f} m: on-axis intensity = {I[N//2, N//2]:.3f} "
          f"(incident intensity at the disc rim = {np.exp(-2*(a_disk/w_ill)**2):.3f})")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


z = 0.05 m: on-axis intensity = 0.799 (incident intensity at the disc rim = 0.801)
z = 0.20 m: on-axis intensity = 0.802 (incident intensity at the disc rim = 0.801)
z = 1.00 m: on-axis intensity = 0.800 (incident intensity at the disc rim = 0.801)








Figure 13.3: A Gaussian beam hitting an opaque 2 mm disc, propagated by the angular-spectrum method. A bright spot appears at the centre of the geometric shadow.





The bright spot in the shadow has the intensity the beam had at the rim of the disc. Poisson considered this prediction absurd; Arago observed it (slide 219).

Slides 277–288: Rayleigh scattering (\(\propto\lambda^{-4}\)), attenuation, fiber loss mechanisms, optical time-domain reflectometry, spontaneous Raman scattering, spontaneous and stimulated Brillouin scattering. A particle much smaller than the wavelength is polarised by the field and re-radiates as an oscillating dipole, in “many” directions (slide 277). \alpha_\text{dB}=\frac{10}{L}\log_{10}\frac{P_\text{in}}{P_\text{out}}=4.34\,\alpha .
\]

14.3 Worked example: a toy OTDR trace (slides 282–283)
An OTDR launches a short pulse and records the Rayleigh backscatter versus time \(t\), that is distance \(z=v_gt/2\). The trace falls with slope \(2\alpha\) (round trip), displayed as \(\alpha\) in dB/km after the conventional 5·log₁₀ scaling. Splices appear as steps and connectors or fiber ends as Fresnel reflection peaks. Chapter 2 has a live OTDR simulator.


Show the Python
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
Ng_f, tau = 1.468, 100e-9
dz = c0*tau/(2*Ng_f)
z = np.arange(0, 30e3, 2.0)
loss = 0.20/1e3*z + 0.15*(z > 8e3) + 0.5*(z > 15e3)
lin = np.where(z <= 25e3, 10**(-loss/10), 0.0)
for z0, hgt in {15e3: 14, 25e3: 18}.items():
    lin += 10**((-np.interp(z0, z, loss) + hgt)/10)*np.exp(-((z - z0)/dz)**2)
lin += 10**(-12/10)
trace = 10*np.log10(lin) + 0.05*rng.standard_normal(z.size)*(1 + (z/10e3)**2)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(); ax.plot(z/1e3, trace, lw=0.7)
ax.set(xlabel="distance (km)", ylabel="relative level (dB)", title=f"resolution ≈ {dz:.0f} m"); plt.show()

15.1 The question
Poynting’s theorem, and why it still works where there is no current. A companion to slides 70–78 and Chapter 3.
We say that light from the Sun heats the Earth, that a radio transmitter “sends power” to a receiver, and that a laser can cut steel. All of these statements assume that energy travels through empty space carried by the electromagnetic field.
That is not obvious. In the gap between the Sun and the Earth there are no charges and no currents. So what exactly is carrying the energy, and how can we prove it rather than just assert it?
The plan is:

section: 15.2 Starting point: how fields exchange energy with matter
text:
15.2 Starting point: how fields exchange energy with matter
Energy, in mechanics, is defined through work. So we first ask: at what rate do electromagnetic fields do work on charges?
A charge \(q\) moving with velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) feels the Lorentz force
\[
\mathbf{F} = q\left(\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}\right).
\]
The power delivered to the charge is
\[
P = \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{v} = q\,\mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{v} + q\,(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B})\cdot\mathbf{v} = q\,\mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{v},
\]
because \(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{v}\): the magnetic force does no work.
For a continuous distribution of charge with density \(\rho\) moving with velocity \(\mathbf{v}\), the current density is \(\mathbf{J}=\rho\mathbf{v}\), and the power delivered per unit volume is
\[
p = \rho\,\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}.
\tag{15.1}\]






ImportantKey point 1



\(\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\) is the only place where the fields hand energy to matter (kinetic energy, heat in a resistor, charging a battery) or take it back (a generator driving an antenna). It is the bridge between “field” and “mechanical energy”.

text:
15.3 Deriving Poynting’s theorem

15.3.1 The two curl equations
\[
\nabla\times\mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}
\tag{15.2}\]
\[
\nabla\times\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J} + \frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}
\tag{15.3}\]


15.3.2 Build a scalar equation
Take the dot product of Equation 15.2 with \(\mathbf{H}\) and of Equation 15.3 with \(\mathbf{E}\):
\[
\mathbf{H}\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{E}) = -\mathbf{H}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}
\]
\[
\mathbf{E}\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{H}) = \mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{J} + \mathbf{E}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}
\]
Subtract the second from the first:
\[
\mathbf{H}\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{E}) - \mathbf{E}\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{H})
= -\mathbf{H}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t} - \mathbf{E}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t} - \mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}.
\]


15.3.3 Use the vector identity
\[
\nabla\cdot(\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H}) = \mathbf{H}\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{E}) - \mathbf{E}\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{H})
\]
The left-hand side is therefore a divergence:
\[
-\nabla\cdot(\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H})
= \mathbf{H}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t} + \mathbf{E}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t} + \mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}.
\tag{15.4}\]


15.3.4 Recognise a time derivative
In a linear, isotropic, non-dispersive medium, \(\mathbf{D}=\varepsilon\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}=\mu\mathbf{H}\) with constant \(\varepsilon,\mu\). Then
\[
\mathbf{E}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t} = \varepsilon\,\mathbf{E}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\tfrac12\varepsilon E^2\right),
\qquad
\mathbf{H}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\tfrac12\mu H^2\right).
\]
Define
\[
u = \tfrac12\left(\mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{D} + \mathbf{H}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right),
\qquad
\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H}.
\tag{15.5}\]






NoteAssumption to keep in mind



The step \(\mathbf{E}\cdot\partial_t\mathbf{D} = \partial_t(\tfrac12\varepsilon E^2)\) assumes a non-dispersive medium. We come back to this in Section 15.9, where it changes the answer to “how fast does energy travel?”.


Equation 15.4 becomes Poynting’s theorem in differential form:
\[
\boxed{\;\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot\mathbf{S} = -\,\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\;}
\tag{15.6}\]


15.3.5 Integral form
Integrate over a volume \(V\) with closed surface \(\partial V\) and apply the divergence theorem:
\[
\boxed{\;-\frac{d}{dt}\int_V u\,dV = \oint_{\partial V}\mathbf{S}\cdot d\mathbf{a} + \int_V \mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\,dV\;}
\tag{15.7}\]






WarningSo far, this is only mathematics



Equation 15.6 is an identity that follows from Maxwell’s equations. We named the quantities \(u\) and \(\mathbf{S}\), but naming is not proving. The physics enters only when we interpret each term.




15.3.6 Interpreting the terms
Read Equation 15.7 as a budget for the volume \(V\):








Term
Meaning
Justified by




\(\int_V \mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\,dV\)
rate at which mechanical energy of charges in \(V\) increases
Lorentz force, Equation 15.1


\(\dfrac{d}{dt}\int_V u\,dV\)
rate of change of something stored in \(V\)
must be energy, for the budget to balance


\(\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf{S}\cdot d\mathbf{a}\)
rate at which that something leaves through the surface
must be energy flux, for the budget to balance



Because the first term is certainly energy per unit time, and all terms in one equation must have the same physical nature, the other two are energy too: \(u\) is the energy density of the field (J/m³) and \(\mathbf{S}\) is the energy flux density (W/m²), the Poynting vector.

section: 15.4 The objection: in vacuum there is no current
text:
15.4 The objection: in vacuum there is no current






TipThe students’ question



“In a wave travelling through empty space there are no electrons. So \(\mathbf{J}=0\). How can a term that needs moving charges tell us anything about the wave?”


The objection is correct. In vacuum, \(\mathbf{J}=0\), \(\mathbf{D}=\varepsilon_0\mathbf{E}\), \(\mathbf{B}=\mu_0\mathbf{H}\), and Equation 15.6 reduces to
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot\mathbf{S} = 0,
\qquad
u = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0 E^2 + \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}.
\tag{15.8}\]
The resolution is to separate two different questions that are easy to mix up.

15.4.1 Question A: in vacuum, is something conserved and moving?
Yes. Equation 15.8 has exactly the form of the continuity equation for charge,
\[
\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot\mathbf{J} = 0 .
\]
It says: \(u\) cannot be created or destroyed at a point; it can only flow, and \(\mathbf{S}\) is its flux. If \(u\) decreases somewhere, it is because \(\mathbf{S}\) carries it to the neighbouring region.


15.4.2 Question B: is that “something” energy?
The vacuum equation alone cannot answer this. A continuity equation only tells you that some quantity is conserved. In fact the free Maxwell equations have other locally conserved quantities built from the fields (for example the optical helicity), each with its own continuity equation. Nothing in Equation 15.8 singles out \(u\) as energy.






NoteGoing further (optional)





Besides energy, momentum and angular momentum, the source-free Maxwell equations admit further conserved densities: the optical helicity, and an infinite family discovered by Lipkin (1964) that he called “zilch”. They are all conserved in vacuum and obey continuity equations, yet none of them is energy. This is precisely why the vacuum equation alone is not enough.





15.4.3 Answer: matter tells us which conserved quantity is energy
“Energy” is defined by what it can do to matter: heat an absorber, accelerate a charge, drive a current. The only term in the theorem that talks to matter is \(\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\), and it only appears where there are charges.
So we apply Equation 15.7 to a volume that contains charges: the transmitting antenna or the absorbing receiver. There, mechanical energy lost or gained by the charges is balanced by \(\mathbf{S}\) and \(u\). That calibrates \(u\) and \(\mathbf{S}\) as energy.
Crucially, \(u\) and \(\mathbf{S}\) are defined by the same expressions Equation 15.5 everywhere, in the antenna and in the empty space around it. Once they are identified as energy where matter is present, they are energy everywhere.






ImportantKey point 2



\(\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\) is not needed where the wave is. It is needed where we identify what the wave carries: at the source and at the receiver. The vacuum region only has to show that the quantity is conserved and moves, which Equation 15.8 does.








TipAn analogy



A ball flying through the air has no force doing work on it (ignore gravity and drag). Nothing during the flight tells you that \(\tfrac12 mv^2\) is energy. You know it because of the throw (your muscles did work) and the impact (it can break a window). The flight only shows that the quantity is conserved and travels with the ball.

15.5 The decisive thought experiment: a pulse in flight
This argument shows that the energy must be in the field, not as a matter of interpretation, but because otherwise energy conservation would fail.

15.5.1 Set-up

A transmitting antenna T at the origin.
A receiver R at distance \(d\).
Empty space in between: no charges, \(\mathbf{J}=0\).

At \(t=0\) the generator drives T for a short time \(\tau\), then switches off. We choose \(\tau \ll d/c\).
We track three volumes: \(V_T\) around the transmitter, \(V_R\) around the receiver, and the vacuum between them.


15.5.2 The energy budget over time
Let \(W_\text{rad}\) be the energy the generator supplied and that did not end up as heat in the antenna wires (it is measurable: it is the work done against the radiation resistance, \(\int R_\text{rad}\,I^2\,dt\)).

15.5.3 The contradiction, and its only resolution
Look at the third row. The transmitter has already lost \(W_\text{rad}\): the generator is switched off and the work has been done. The receiver has not yet gained anything, because no signal travels faster than \(c\). Between them there is no matter at all.
If energy is only a property of matter, then during the interval \(\tau < t < d/c\) the total energy of the universe is smaller by \(W_\text{rad}\). Energy conservation would be violated for a finite time, and then mysteriously restored when the pulse arrives.
The only way to keep energy conserved at every instant is that the energy is located in the fields between T and R. Poynting’s theorem tells us exactly where and how much. At time \(t\) the pulse occupies the spherical shell \(c(t-\tau) < r < ct\), and
\[
\int_\text{shell} u\,dV = W_\text{rad}.
\]






ImportantKey point 3



The absence of current in the vacuum is not a weakness of the argument. It is the argument. Because nothing material sits between transmitter and receiver while the pulse is in flight, the energy has nowhere else to be but in the field.

text:
15.6 A common trap: the “displacement current”
In vacuum Equation 15.3 reads
\[
\nabla\times\mathbf{H} = \varepsilon_0\frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t}.
\]
The right-hand side is historically called the displacement current. Some students conclude: “So there is a current in vacuum, and that is what \(\mathbf{J}\) refers to.” This is wrong, for two reasons.

It involves no moving charge. It is simply a time-varying electric field. The name comes from Maxwell’s mechanical models of the ether and is misleading.
In the derivation it does not end up in \(\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\). It ends up in \(\mathbf{E}\cdot\partial\mathbf{D}/\partial t\), which is part of \(\partial u/\partial t\): it describes a change of stored field energy, not work done on matter.

\(\mathbf{J}\) in Poynting’s theorem is always the current of real charges.

text:
15.7 Plane waves from Maxwell’s equations
Up to now we have stated the plane-wave fields. Here we derive them, and in particular the relation \(E = vB\), which is what makes the electric and magnetic energies equal.






NoteConvention



We use the physics convention \(e^{i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}-\omega t)}\). With the engineering convention \(e^{j(\omega t-\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r})}\) the signs of some intermediate expressions change (for example \(\varepsilon - j\sigma/\omega\) instead of \(\varepsilon + i\sigma/\omega\)), but every physical result is identical. Physical fields are always the real parts of the complex expressions.



15.7.1 Ansatz
Consider a linear, homogeneous, isotropic, source-free medium (\(\rho=0\), \(\mathbf{J}=0\)) with constant \(\varepsilon\) and \(\mu\). We look for solutions of the form
\[
\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r},t) = \mathbf{E}_0\,e^{i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}-\omega t)},
\qquad
\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r},t) = \mathbf{B}_0\,e^{i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}-\omega t)},
\tag{15.9}\]
where \(\mathbf{E}_0\) and \(\mathbf{B}_0\) are constant vectors, possibly complex (this includes every polarization).
For such fields, derivatives become multiplications:
\[
\nabla \;\to\; i\mathbf{k},
\qquad
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \;\to\; -i\omega .
\]
Maxwell’s four differential equations therefore become four algebraic vector equations.


15.7.2 The divergence equations: the wave is transverse
\[
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{E}_0 = 0,
\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{B}_0 = 0 .
\]
Both fields are perpendicular to the direction of propagation.


15.7.3 Faraday’s law: the ratio \(E/B\)
\[
\nabla\times\mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}
\;\Rightarrow\;
i\,\mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{E}_0 = i\omega\,\mathbf{B}_0
\;\Rightarrow\;
\boxed{\;\mathbf{B}_0 = \frac{\mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{E}_0}{\omega}\;}
\tag{15.10}\]
This single line contains three results.

Direction. \(\mathbf{B}_0\) is perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{E}_0\) and \(\mathbf{k}\): the vectors \((\mathbf{E},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{k})\) form a right-handed triad.
Magnitude. Since \(\mathbf{k}\perp\mathbf{E}_0\), \(|\mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{E}_0| = k\,|\mathbf{E}_0|\), hence \[
\frac{|\mathbf{E}_0|}{|\mathbf{B}_0|} = \frac{\omega}{k} \equiv v_\varphi ,
\] the phase velocity. This is the precise meaning of \(v\) in “\(E = vB\)”.
Phase. If \(k\) is real, \(\mathbf{B}\) is exactly in phase with \(\mathbf{E}\): they vanish and peak at the same points and instants.







ImportantKey point 4



Faraday’s law alone relates \(E\) and \(B\), but it does not tell us how fast the wave travels: \(v_\varphi\) is still unknown.




15.7.4 Ampère–Maxwell law: a second relation
\[
\nabla\times\mathbf{H} = \frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}
\;\Rightarrow\;
i\,\mathbf{k}\times\frac{\mathbf{B}_0}{\mu} = -i\omega\varepsilon\,\mathbf{E}_0
\;\Rightarrow\;
\mathbf{E}_0 = -\frac{\mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{B}_0}{\omega\mu\varepsilon} .
\tag{15.11}\]


15.7.5 Consistency: the dispersion relation
Insert Equation 15.10 into Equation 15.11:
\[
\mathbf{E}_0 = -\frac{\mathbf{k}\times(\mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{E}_0)}{\omega^2\mu\varepsilon} .
\]
With \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})\) and \(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{E}_0 = 0\),
\[
\mathbf{k}\times(\mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{E}_0) = \mathbf{k}\,(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{E}_0) - k^2\,\mathbf{E}_0 = -k^2\,\mathbf{E}_0 ,
\]
so
\[
\mathbf{E}_0 = \frac{k^2}{\omega^2\mu\varepsilon}\,\mathbf{E}_0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\boxed{\;k^2 = \omega^2\mu\varepsilon\;}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
v_\varphi = \frac{\omega}{k} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}} .
\tag{15.12}\]
In vacuum \(v_\varphi = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0} = c\), and therefore \(E = cB\).






ImportantKey point 5



Faraday says \(E/B = \omega/k\). Ampère–Maxwell says \(E/B = k/(\omega\mu\varepsilon)\). Both can be true only if the wave travels at \(1/\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}\). Neither equation alone predicts light; their mutual consistency does.




15.7.6 Back to real fields
Take \(\mathbf{k} = k\,\hat{\mathbf{z}}\) and \(\mathbf{E}_0 = E_0\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) with \(E_0\) real. Then \(\mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{E}_0 = kE_0\,\hat{\mathbf{y}}\), and the real parts are
\[
\mathbf{E} = E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf{x}},
\qquad
\mathbf{B} = \frac{E_0}{v_\varphi}\cos(kz-\omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf{y}} .
\tag{15.13}\]
Because Equation 15.10 is linear, the same holds for any polarization. For circular polarization, \(\mathbf{E}_0 = E_0(\hat{\mathbf{x}} + i\hat{\mathbf{y}})/\sqrt2\): \(\mathbf{B}\) rotates together with \(\mathbf{E}\), always at \(90^\circ\) from it, with \(|\mathbf{E}| = v_\varphi|\mathbf{B}|\) at every instant.


15.7.7 Energy of the plane wave
With \(H = B/\mu\) and \(E = v_\varphi B\):
\[
u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu} = \frac{E^2}{2\mu v_\varphi^2} = \tfrac12\varepsilon E^2 = u_E,
\qquad
\frac{E}{H} = \mu v_\varphi = \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}} \equiv \eta ,
\]
where \(\eta\) is the wave impedance (\(\eta_0 \approx 377\ \Omega\) in vacuum). The electric and magnetic energy densities are equal, and \(u = \varepsilon E^2\).
The Poynting vector points along \(\mathbf{k}\) (right-handed triad):
\[
\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H} = \frac{E^2}{\eta}\,\hat{\mathbf{k}} = v_\varphi\,u\,\hat{\mathbf{k}} .
\]
Time averages, using phasors and \(\langle\cos^2\rangle = \tfrac12\):
\[
\langle\mathbf{S}\rangle = \tfrac12\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left(\mathbf{E}_0\times\mathbf{H}_0^*\right) = \frac{|\mathbf{E}_0|^2}{2\eta}\,\hat{\mathbf{k}},
\qquad
\langle u\rangle = \tfrac12\varepsilon\,|\mathbf{E}_0|^2,
\qquad
\langle S\rangle = v_\varphi\,\langle u\rangle .
\tag{15.14}\]
In vacuum the energy flows at \(c\). You can check directly that Equation 15.13 satisfies Equation 15.8.






WarningHold on



In a non-dispersive medium the energy moves at the phase velocity. We will see in Section 15.9 that this is not true in dispersive media: there, energy moves at the group velocity.

section: 15.8 Plane waves in a lossy medium
text:
15.8 Plane waves in a lossy medium
We now put charges back in: a medium with conductivity \(\sigma\), so that \(\mathbf{J} = \sigma\mathbf{E}\). This is exactly the situation of the receiver (the absorber) in the pulse thought experiment, and it is where \(\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\) becomes non-zero.

15.8.1 Complex permittivity and complex wave number
Ampère–Maxwell now reads
\[
i\,\mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{H}_0 = \sigma\mathbf{E}_0 - i\omega\varepsilon\,\mathbf{E}_0 = -i\omega\,\varepsilon_c\,\mathbf{E}_0,
\qquad
\varepsilon_c \equiv \varepsilon + i\frac{\sigma}{\omega} .
\tag{15.15}\]
The conduction current is absorbed into a complex permittivity \(\varepsilon_c\). Faraday’s law is unchanged, so every step of Section 15.7 goes through with \(\varepsilon \to \varepsilon_c\):
\[
k^2 = \omega^2\mu\,\varepsilon_c .
\]
The wave number is now complex. For a wave travelling along \(z\) we write
\[
k = \beta + i\alpha,
\qquad
\beta^2 - \alpha^2 = \omega^2\mu\varepsilon,
\qquad
2\alpha\beta = \omega\mu\sigma ,
\tag{15.16}\]
which gives
\[
\beta = \omega\sqrt{\frac{\mu\varepsilon}{2}}\left[\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon}\right)^2}+1\right]^{1/2},
\qquad
\alpha = \omega\sqrt{\frac{\mu\varepsilon}{2}}\left[\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon}\right)^2}-1\right]^{1/2}.
\]
The dimensionless ratio \(\sigma/(\omega\varepsilon)\) (conduction current over displacement current) decides the regime.


15.8.2 The fields
With \(\mathbf{E}_0 = E_0\hat{\mathbf{x}}\), \(E_0\) real:
\[
\mathbf{E} = E_0\,e^{-\alpha z}\cos(\beta z - \omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf{x}} .
\]
Faraday still gives \(\mathbf{B}_0 = \mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{E}_0/\omega\), but now \(k\) is complex:
\[
B_0 = \frac{\beta + i\alpha}{\omega}\,E_0 = \frac{|k|}{\omega}\,E_0\,e^{i\phi},
\qquad
\phi = \arctan\frac{\alpha}{\beta},
\]
\[
\mathbf{B} = \frac{|k|}{\omega}\,E_0\,e^{-\alpha z}\cos(\beta z - \omega t + \phi)\,\hat{\mathbf{y}} .
\]
Three things change with respect to the lossless case:

The wave decays as \(e^{-\alpha z}\); the intensity decays as \(e^{-2\alpha z}\).
\(\mathbf{B}\) lags \(\mathbf{E}\) in time by \(\phi/\omega\).
The simple relation fails: \(|E|/|B| = \omega/|k|\), which is neither \(\omega/\beta\) (the phase velocity) nor \(1/\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}\).



15.8.3 Limiting case: a good conductor
For \(\sigma \gg \omega\varepsilon\):
\[
\alpha \simeq \beta \simeq \sqrt{\frac{\omega\mu\sigma}{2}} \equiv \frac{1}{\delta},
\qquad
\phi \simeq 45^\circ ,
\]
where \(\delta\) is the skin depth. The ratio of magnetic to electric energy is
\[
\frac{\langle u_B\rangle}{\langle u_E\rangle} = \frac{|B_0|^2/\mu}{\varepsilon|E_0|^2} = \frac{|k|^2}{\omega^2\mu\varepsilon} = \sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon}\right)^2} \gg 1 :
\]
inside a good conductor the field energy is almost entirely magnetic, and \(|E|/|H| = \sqrt{\omega\mu/\sigma} \ll \eta_0\).


15.8.4 Poynting’s theorem with \(\mathbf{J}\ne 0\): the absorber’s energy budget
This is the case the pulse argument needs: the field hands its energy to matter. We check Equation 15.6 explicitly.
With \(\mathbf{H}_0 = \mathbf{B}_0/\mu = (\beta + i\alpha)E_0/(\omega\mu)\,\hat{\mathbf{y}}\), the time-averaged Poynting vector is
\[
\langle S_z\rangle = \tfrac12\mathrm{Re}\!\left(E_0 H_0^*\right)e^{-2\alpha z}
= \frac{\beta\,E_0^2}{2\omega\mu}\,e^{-2\alpha z} .
\]
In steady state \(\langle \partial u/\partial t\rangle = 0\), so the time-averaged theorem reads \(-\,d\langle S_z\rangle/dz = \langle\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\rangle\). Both sides:
\[
-\frac{d\langle S_z\rangle}{dz} = \frac{\alpha\beta}{\omega\mu}\,E_0^2\,e^{-2\alpha z},
\qquad
\langle\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\rangle = \langle\sigma E^2\rangle = \tfrac12\sigma E_0^2\,e^{-2\alpha z} .
\]
They are equal because \(2\alpha\beta = \omega\mu\sigma\) (Equation 15.16). ✓
Integrating the Joule heating over the whole half-space \(z>0\):
\[
\int_0^\infty \tfrac12\sigma E_0^2\,e^{-2\alpha z}\,dz = \frac{\sigma E_0^2}{4\alpha} = \frac{\beta E_0^2}{2\omega\mu} = \langle S_z(0)\rangle .
\]






ImportantKey point 6



All the power that enters the surface of the absorber is converted into heat, and Poynting’s theorem accounts for it point by point. The decrease of \(\mathbf{S}\) with depth is exactly the work \(\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\) done on the conduction electrons. This is the “receiver” end of the pulse argument, now made quantitative.


(Here \(E_0\) is the field just inside the surface; the reflection at the interface is a separate problem.)

section: 15.9 Energy velocity and group velocity in dispersive media
text:
15.9 Energy velocity and group velocity in dispersive media

15.9.1 The problem
Real materials are dispersive: \(\varepsilon\) and \(\mu\) depend on frequency. Glass, silicon, lithium niobate: the refractive index \(n(\omega)\) is never exactly constant.
Two things then go wrong with what we did so far.

In the derivation of Poynting’s theorem we wrote \(\mathbf{E}\cdot\partial\mathbf{D}/\partial t = \partial_t(\tfrac12\varepsilon E^2)\). This requires \(\mathbf{D}(t) = \varepsilon\,\mathbf{E}(t)\) at the same instant. In a dispersive medium \(\mathbf{D}(t)\) depends on \(\mathbf{E}\) at earlier times, so \(u = \tfrac12(\mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{D} + \mathbf{H}\cdot\mathbf{B})\) is no longer the stored energy.
A pulse does not travel at the phase velocity \(\omega/k\) but at the group velocity

\[
v_g = \frac{d\omega}{dk} = \frac{c}{n + \omega\,\dfrac{dn}{d\omega}} \equiv \frac{c}{n_g},
\]
where \(n_g\) is the group index. In silicon waveguides, for example, \(n_g\) is typically much larger than the effective index.
We define the energy velocity as the ratio of time-averaged energy flux to time-averaged energy density:
\[
v_E \equiv \frac{\langle S\rangle}{\langle u\rangle} .
\tag{15.17}\]
In Equation 15.14 we found \(v_E = v_\varphi\), but that used the non-dispersive \(u\). The goal of this section is to find the correct \(\langle u\rangle\) and prove that
\[
\boxed{\;v_E = v_g\;}
\]
for any lossless (or weakly lossy) dispersive medium.


15.9.2 Step 1: the stored energy in a dispersive medium (Brillouin)

15.9.2.1 Quasi-monochromatic field
Energy density only makes sense for a field that is switched on and evolves, so consider a carrier at frequency \(\omega\) with a slowly varying complex envelope \(\tilde{\mathbf{E}}(t)\):
\[
\mathbf{E}(t) = \mathrm{Re}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{E}}(t)\,e^{-i\omega t}\right],
\qquad
\left|\frac{d\tilde{\mathbf{E}}}{dt}\right| \ll \omega\,|\tilde{\mathbf{E}}| .
\]
“Slowly varying” means the envelope changes little during one optical period, i.e. the spectrum of \(\tilde{\mathbf{E}}\) is concentrated in a narrow band \(\Omega \ll \omega\) around the carrier.


15.9.2.2 The response of the medium
Write the envelope as a superposition of small frequency offsets, \(\tilde{\mathbf{E}}(t) = \int \tilde{\mathbf{E}}(\Omega)\,e^{-i\Omega t}\,d\Omega\). Each component at \(\omega+\Omega\) is multiplied by \(\varepsilon(\omega+\Omega)\). Expanding to first order,
\[
\varepsilon(\omega+\Omega) \simeq \varepsilon(\omega) + \Omega\,\frac{d\varepsilon}{d\omega} .
\]
Since \(\Omega\,e^{-i\Omega t} = i\,\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{-i\Omega t}\), the factor \(\Omega\) becomes \(i\,d/dt\) acting on the envelope:
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{D}}(t) \simeq \varepsilon\,\tilde{\mathbf{E}} + i\,\frac{d\varepsilon}{d\omega}\,\frac{d\tilde{\mathbf{E}}}{dt} ,
\qquad
\mathbf{D}(t) = \mathrm{Re}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{D}}(t)\,e^{-i\omega t}\right].
\tag{15.18}\]


15.9.2.3 Averaging over one period
\[
\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t} = \mathrm{Re}\!\left[\left(\frac{d\tilde{\mathbf{D}}}{dt} - i\omega\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\right)e^{-i\omega t}\right].
\]
For two slowly varying phasors, \(\langle \mathrm{Re}[\mathbf{a}\,e^{-i\omega t}]\cdot\mathrm{Re}[\mathbf{b}\,e^{-i\omega t}]\rangle = \tfrac12\mathrm{Re}(\mathbf{a}^*\cdot\mathbf{b})\). Keeping terms to first order in \(d/dt\), using Equation 15.18:
\[
\frac{d\tilde{\mathbf{D}}}{dt} - i\omega\tilde{\mathbf{D}}
\simeq -i\omega\varepsilon\,\tilde{\mathbf{E}} + \left(\varepsilon + \omega\frac{d\varepsilon}{d\omega}\right)\frac{d\tilde{\mathbf{E}}}{dt} .
\]
Therefore
\[
\left\langle \mathbf{E}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}\right\rangle
= \tfrac12\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left[-i\omega\varepsilon\,|\tilde{\mathbf{E}}|^2\right]
+ \tfrac12\,\frac{d(\omega\varepsilon)}{d\omega}\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{E}}^*\cdot\frac{d\tilde{\mathbf{E}}}{dt}\right].
\]

If \(\varepsilon\) is real (lossless), the first term vanishes.
In the second term, \(\mathrm{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf{E}}^*\cdot d\tilde{\mathbf{E}}/dt] = \tfrac12\,d|\tilde{\mathbf{E}}|^2/dt\).

So
\[
\left\langle \mathbf{E}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}\right\rangle = \frac{d}{dt}\left[\frac14\,\frac{d(\omega\varepsilon)}{d\omega}\,|\tilde{\mathbf{E}}|^2\right],
\]
and identically for the magnetic term. The time-averaged stored energy density is the Brillouin formula:
\[
\boxed{\;\langle u\rangle = \frac14\left[\frac{d(\omega\varepsilon)}{d\omega}\,|\tilde{\mathbf{E}}|^2 + \frac{d(\omega\mu)}{d\omega}\,|\tilde{\mathbf{H}}|^2\right]\;}
\tag{15.19}\]
For a non-dispersive medium, \(d(\omega\varepsilon)/d\omega = \varepsilon\) and we recover \(\langle u\rangle = \tfrac14(\varepsilon|E|^2 + \mu|H|^2)\), consistent with Equation 15.14.






NoteWhat about losses?



If \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_R + i\varepsilon_I\), the first term no longer vanishes and gives \(\tfrac12\omega\varepsilon_I|\tilde{\mathbf{E}}|^2\), which is not a time derivative. It is a dissipation term, identical to \(\langle\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\rangle\) with an effective conductivity \(\sigma = \omega\varepsilon_I\), exactly as in Equation 15.15. The Brillouin formula is meaningful when \(\varepsilon_I \ll \varepsilon_R\), i.e. away from absorption lines.





15.9.3 Step 2: what the extra energy is (a check with the Lorentz model)
Why should the stored energy contain \(d\varepsilon/d\omega\)? Because in a material, part of the energy is mechanical energy of the bound charges. The polarization current \(\partial\mathbf{P}/\partial t\) is a current of real (bound) charges, so it does work \(\mathbf{E}\cdot\partial\mathbf{P}/\partial t\): this is the \(\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\) idea again, now hidden inside \(\mathbf{D}\).
Take the lossless Lorentz model: \(N\) oscillators per unit volume, charge \(q\), mass \(m\), resonance \(\omega_r\),
\[
m\ddot{x} = -m\omega_r^2 x + qE
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
x_0 = \frac{q E_0}{m(\omega_r^2-\omega^2)},
\qquad
\varepsilon(\omega) = \varepsilon_0\left[1 + \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega_r^2-\omega^2}\right],
\qquad
\omega_p^2 = \frac{Nq^2}{m\varepsilon_0}.
\]
Mechanical energy of the oscillators, time-averaged:
\[
\langle u_\text{mech}\rangle = N\left\langle \tfrac12 m\dot{x}^2 + \tfrac12 m\omega_r^2 x^2\right\rangle
= \frac14 N m(\omega^2+\omega_r^2)\,|x_0|^2
= \frac14\,\varepsilon_0\,\omega_p^2\,\frac{\omega_r^2+\omega^2}{(\omega_r^2-\omega^2)^2}\,|E_0|^2 .
\]
Brillouin electric term:
\[
\frac{d(\omega\varepsilon)}{d\omega} = \varepsilon_0\left[1 + \omega_p^2\,\frac{\omega_r^2+\omega^2}{(\omega_r^2-\omega^2)^2}\right]
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\frac14\,\frac{d(\omega\varepsilon)}{d\omega}\,|E_0|^2
= \underbrace{\frac14\varepsilon_0|E_0|^2}_{\text{vacuum field}} + \underbrace{\langle u_\text{mech}\rangle}_{\text{bound charges}} .
\]






ImportantKey point 7



The Brillouin energy density is vacuum field energy plus the kinetic and potential energy of the bound charges that the wave sets in motion. The naive expression \(\tfrac14\varepsilon|E|^2\) misses the latter; it can even become negative where \(\varepsilon<0\), which is physically meaningless. For a passive lossless medium \(d(\omega\varepsilon)/d\omega > 0\) always (the electromagnetic analogue of Foster’s reactance theorem), so the Brillouin energy is always positive.




15.9.4 Step 3: proof that \(v_E = v_g\)
Take a plane wave in a lossless medium with real \(\varepsilon(\omega)\) and \(\mu(\omega)\). We use the prime for \(d/d\omega\) in this subsection only.
Energy flux. With \(|H_0| = |E_0|/\eta\) and \(\eta = \sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}\):
\[
\langle S\rangle = \frac{|E_0|^2}{2\eta} = \frac12\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu}}\,|E_0|^2 .
\]
Energy density. From Equation 15.19, with \(|H_0|^2 = (\varepsilon/\mu)|E_0|^2\):
\[
\langle u\rangle = \frac14|E_0|^2\left[(\varepsilon + \omega\varepsilon') + \frac{\varepsilon}{\mu}(\mu + \omega\mu')\right]
= \frac{\varepsilon}{4}|E_0|^2\left[2 + \omega\frac{\varepsilon'}{\varepsilon} + \omega\frac{\mu'}{\mu}\right].
\]
Inverse group velocity. From \(k = \omega\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}\):
\[
\frac{dk}{d\omega} = \sqrt{\mu\varepsilon} + \omega\,\frac{\mu\varepsilon' + \varepsilon\mu'}{2\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}}
= \frac{\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}}{2}\left[2 + \omega\frac{\varepsilon'}{\varepsilon} + \omega\frac{\mu'}{\mu}\right].
\]
Compare. The same bracket appears in both. Eliminating it:
\[
\langle u\rangle = \frac{\varepsilon}{4}|E_0|^2\cdot\frac{2}{\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}}\,\frac{dk}{d\omega}
= \frac12\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu}}\,|E_0|^2\,\frac{dk}{d\omega}
= \langle S\rangle\,\frac{dk}{d\omega} .
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\;v_E = \frac{\langle S\rangle}{\langle u\rangle} = \frac{d\omega}{dk} = v_g\;}
\tag{15.20}\]






ImportantKey point 8



In a dispersive, lossless medium, energy is transported at the group velocity, not at the phase velocity. The extra term \(\omega\,d\varepsilon/d\omega\) in the stored energy (the energy parked in the bound charges) is exactly what slows the energy down from \(v_\varphi\) to \(v_g\). In a non-dispersive medium the two coincide, which is why Equation 15.14 gave \(v_\varphi\).




15.9.5 How general is this?
The result is not limited to isotropic plane waves. For lossless systems it also holds for:

Anisotropic media. The energy velocity is the vector \(\mathbf{v}_E = \nabla_{\mathbf{k}}\,\omega(\mathbf{k})\), which in general is not parallel to \(\mathbf{k}\). This is why the ray direction and the wave-vector direction differ in birefringent crystals.
Waveguides. With \(\beta(\omega)\) the propagation constant of a mode, the ratio of guided power to energy per unit length equals \(d\omega/d\beta\), both in metallic waveguides and in dielectric (photonic) waveguides, where the dispersion comes from both material and geometry.
Periodic structures (photonic crystals, gratings). For Bloch modes, with flux and energy averaged over one unit cell, the energy velocity equals \(\nabla_{\mathbf{k}}\,\omega\) of the band. Near a band edge \(v_g\to 0\), which is the basis of slow-light devices.
Negative-index media. \(v_g\) is antiparallel to \(\mathbf{k}\), but \(\langle\mathbf{S}\rangle\) is antiparallel too: the equality still holds.



15.9.6 When it fails: the “weird cases”
The identification \(v_E = v_g\) rests on two assumptions: negligible loss and a first-order Taylor expansion of \(\varepsilon(\omega)\) over the pulse bandwidth. It breaks down when either fails.

Near an absorption line (anomalous dispersion). There \(dn/d\omega < 0\), and \(v_g = c/n_g\) can exceed \(c\), become infinite or even negative. This does not violate causality: the medium reshapes the pulse by absorbing more of its trailing part, so the peak appears to advance, but no energy or information travels faster than \(c\). A proper energy velocity that includes the energy stored in and dissipated by the oscillators stays below \(c\) (Loudon, 1970). The front of a signal always travels at \(c\) (Sommerfeld and Brillouin).
Strong higher-order dispersion. If \(\varepsilon(\omega)\) curves significantly over the pulse bandwidth, the pulse distorts and “the velocity of the pulse” is no longer well defined. The equality \(v_E = v_g\) still holds frequency by frequency, but \(v_g\) at the carrier no longer describes where the energy of the whole pulse is.
Evanescent waves and tunnelling. When \(k\) is imaginary, \(d\omega/dk\) loses its meaning as a velocity; apparent superluminal tunnelling times (the Hartman effect) are another manifestation.







TipFor a classroom



A good conceptual summary: phase velocity is how fast the crests move, group velocity is how fast the envelope moves, and in a transparent medium the energy rides with the envelope. The “weird cases” are all situations where the medium is not transparent, or where the envelope itself stops being a well-defined object.

section: 15.10 Radiation: energy that never comes back
text:
15.10 Radiation: energy that never comes back
For a localised oscillating source (an antenna), the fields far away decrease as \(1/r\). Then \(|\mathbf{S}|\propto 1/r^2\), and the power through a sphere of radius \(r\),
\[
P = \oint_{r}\mathbf{S}\cdot d\mathbf{a} \;\propto\; \frac{1}{r^2}\cdot r^2 = \text{constant},
\]
does not depend on \(r\). The same power crosses every sphere, however large: energy leaves the source and never returns. This is what distinguishes a radiated wave from the near-field terms, which decrease faster than \(1/r\) and only exchange energy back and forth with the source.

title: 15  Deep dive: does an electromagnetic wave carry energy?
text:
15.11 Experimental confirmation
The argument above is theoretical. Experiments confirm it in two independent ways.

Heating. An absorber (bolometer, thermopile, optical power meter) placed in a beam warms up. Its temperature rise gives the absorbed power, and it matches \(\oint\mathbf{S}\cdot d\mathbf{a}\).
Radiation pressure. The field also carries momentum, with density \(\mathbf{S}/c^2\). A beam of power \(P\) exerts a force \(P/c\) on an absorber and \(2P/c\) on a mirror. This was measured by Lebedev (1900) and by Nichols and Hull (1901 to 1903).

title: 15  Deep dive: does an electromagnetic wave carry energy?
text:
15.12 Summary






ImportantThe logic in seven steps




Energy is defined by work on matter. The fields do work on charges at the rate \(\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\) per unit volume.
Maxwell’s equations imply Poynting’s theorem, \(\partial_t u + \nabla\cdot\mathbf{S} = -\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\). Where charges are present, the budget identifies \(u\) and \(\mathbf{S}\) as energy density and energy flux.
In vacuum, \(\mathbf{J}=0\) and the theorem becomes a continuity equation: the same quantity \(u\) is conserved and flows with flux \(\mathbf{S}\). It is energy because it is the same \(u\) that was identified at the source.
Pulse argument. While a pulse is between transmitter and receiver, the transmitter has lost energy and the receiver has gained none. Energy conservation at every instant requires the energy to be in the field.
Plane waves. Faraday gives \(E/B = \omega/k\) and Ampère–Maxwell fixes \(\omega/k = 1/\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}\); electric and magnetic energies are equal.
Absorbers. In a lossy medium, the decrease of \(\mathbf{S}\) with depth equals the Joule heating \(\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\): the field’s energy is handed over to matter.
Dispersive media. The stored energy includes the energy of the bound charges (Brillouin), and energy travels at the group velocity, \(v_E = d\omega/dk\), except near absorption lines and in other strongly non-transparent situations.

title: 15  Deep dive: does an electromagnetic wave carry energy?
text:
15.13 Questions for discussion






TipQ1. Why does the magnetic field never appear in the power delivered to charges?





Because \(q(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B})\cdot\mathbf{v}=0\): the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity. The magnetic field still stores energy (\(B^2/2\mu_0\)) and contributes to \(\mathbf{S}\), but it transfers energy to matter only indirectly, through the electric field it induces.









TipQ2. In vacuum \(\mathbf{J}=0\). Does Poynting’s theorem become useless there?





No. It becomes a continuity equation, which shows that \(u\) is conserved locally and flows with flux \(\mathbf{S}\). What it cannot do by itself is tell us that \(u\) is energy; that identification comes from regions with charges.









TipQ3. Is the displacement current \(\varepsilon_0\,\partial\mathbf{E}/\partial t\) part of \(\mathbf{J}\)?





No. It contains no moving charges and contributes to \(\partial u/\partial t\) (change of stored field energy), not to \(\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}\) (work on matter).









TipQ4. In the pulse experiment, why is it important that \(\tau \ll d/c\)?





So that there is a finite time interval in which the transmitter has completely stopped and the receiver has not yet been reached. During that interval no matter anywhere holds the missing energy, which makes the contradiction unavoidable.









TipQ5. For a plane wave, show that \(\langle S\rangle = c\langle u\rangle\). What does this ratio mean physically?





See Section 15.7. The ratio of flux to density has dimensions of velocity: it is the speed at which energy is transported, here \(c\).









TipQ6. In a good conductor, is the field energy mainly electric or magnetic? Why?





Mainly magnetic: \(\langle u_B\rangle/\langle u_E\rangle = \sqrt{1+(\sigma/\omega\varepsilon)^2} \gg 1\). The conduction current \(\sigma E\) is much larger than the displacement current, so a small \(E\) sustains a large \(H\) through Ampère’s law.









TipQ7. Why does \(\tfrac12\varepsilon E^2\) fail as an energy density in a dispersive medium?





Because \(\mathbf{D}(t)\) depends on the past values of \(\mathbf{E}\), so \(\mathbf{E}\cdot\partial_t\mathbf{D}\) is not the time derivative of \(\tfrac12\varepsilon E^2\). Physically, the formula ignores the kinetic and potential energy of the bound charges driven by the wave (Section 15.9).









TipQ8. A hollow metallic waveguide has \(\beta = \sqrt{\omega^2/c^2 - \omega_c^2/c^2}\). Compute \(v_\varphi\) and \(v_g\). Which one can exceed \(c\), and which one carries the energy?





\(v_\varphi = \omega/\beta = c/\sqrt{1-\omega_c^2/\omega^2} > c\) and \(v_g = d\omega/d\beta = c\sqrt{1-\omega_c^2/\omega^2} < c\), with \(v_\varphi v_g = c^2\). The energy travels at \(v_g\); the phase velocity exceeding \(c\) carries no energy or information.









TipQ9. Near an absorption line the group velocity can exceed \(c\). Does energy travel faster than light?





No. The medium absorbs the trailing part of the pulse more strongly, which moves the peak forward without any energy getting ahead of the front. The assumptions behind \(v_E = v_g\) (negligible loss, slowly varying \(\varepsilon\) over the bandwidth) fail there.

pip install -r requirements.txt     # numpy scipy matplotlib pandas jupyter ipywidgets (+ optional packages)

A.3 Publishing the website (GitHub Pages)
The source lives at https://github.com/philippevelha/Optoelectronics-teaching (folder chapter1/) and the site at https://philippevelha.github.io/Optoelectronics-teaching/chapter1/. After editing a chapter:
cd notebooks && python build_notebooks.py && cd ..         # refresh the notebooks (Colab buttons point to them)
git add -A && git commit -m "Update chapter 1" && git push   # update the source on GitHub
bash ../publish.sh                                         # render and update the website

title: Appendix B — Formula sheet
text:
B.13 Typical numbers worth remembering
All the key relations of Chapter 1 on one page. Each block links to the chapter where the formula is derived and used. SI units; engineering convention \(e^{j(\omega t-kz)}\), \(N=n-jK\). Use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF for a paper copy.

title: Appendix B — Formula sheet
text:
B.1 Waves (Chapter 1)







plane wave
\(E_x=E_0\cos(\omega t-kz+\phi_0)\)


wave vector form
\(E=E_0\cos(\omega t-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r+\phi_0)\)


phase velocity
\(v=\omega/k=\nu\lambda=c/n\)


phase change over \(\Delta z\)
\(\Delta\phi=k\,\Delta z=2\pi\Delta z/\lambda\)


in a medium
\(\lambda_\text{medium}=\lambda/n\), \(\ k_\text{medium}=nk\)


photon energy
\(E=h\nu=hc/\lambda\) (\(1.24/\lambda[\mu\text{m}]\) eV)


spectral width
\(\Delta\lambda=\lambda^2\Delta\nu/c\) (100 GHz ↔︎ 0.8 nm at 1550 nm)


spherical wave
amplitude \(\propto1/r\), irradiance \(\propto1/r^2\)

title: Appendix B — Formula sheet
text:
B.2 Gaussian beams (Chapter 2)







irradiance
\(I(r,z)=\dfrac{2P}{\pi w^2}e^{-2r^2/w^2}\)


beam radius
\(w(z)=w_0\sqrt{1+(z/z_0)^2}\)


Rayleigh range
\(z_0=\pi w_0^2n/\lambda\)


divergence
\(\theta=\lambda/(\pi w_0)\); real beams \(2\theta=M^2\dfrac{4\lambda}{\pi(2w_0)}\)


wavefront radius
\(R(z)=z[1+(z_0/z)^2]\)


power inside \(r=w\)
\(1-e^{-2}\approx86\,\%\)


ABCD law
\(q=z+jz_0\), \(\ q'=\dfrac{Aq+B}{Cq+D}\)


Gaussian coupling
\(\eta=\left(\dfrac{2w_1w_2}{w_1^2+w_2^2}\right)^2e^{-2d^2/(w_1^2+w_2^2)}\)

title: Appendix B — Formula sheet
text:
B.3 Irradiance (Chapter 3)







magnetic field
\(B=E/v\)


energy density
\(u=\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_rE^2\)


Poynting vector
\(\mathbf S=v^2\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r\,\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\)


average irradiance
\(I=\tfrac12c\,\varepsilon_0nE_0^2\)


Gaussian peak
\(I_0=2P/(\pi w_0^2)\)


isotropic source
\(I=P/(4\pi r^2)\)

title: Appendix B — Formula sheet
text:
B.4 Refractive index and absorption (Chapter 4)







index
\(n=\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}\) (at the optical frequency)


Sellmeier
\(n^2=1+\sum_i\dfrac{A_i\lambda^2}{\lambda^2-\lambda_i^2}\)


Lorentz oscillator
\(\varepsilon_r=1+\dfrac{\omega_p^2}{\omega_0^2-\omega^2+j\gamma\omega}\), \(\ \omega_p^2=\dfrac{Ne^2}{\varepsilon_0m}\)


Drude (metals)
Lorentz with \(\omega_0=0\)


complex index
\(N=n-jK\), \(\ n^2-K^2=\varepsilon_r'\), \(\ 2nK=\varepsilon_r''\)


absorption
\(\alpha=4\pi K/\lambda\), \(\ I=I_0e^{-\alpha z}\)


reflectance
\(R=\dfrac{(n-1)^2+K^2}{(n+1)^2+K^2}\)


Kramers–Kronig
\(\varepsilon_r'-1=\dfrac2\pi\mathcal P\!\int_0^\infty\dfrac{\omega'\varepsilon_r''(\omega')}{\omega'^2-\omega^2}d\omega'\)

title: Appendix B — Formula sheet
text:
B.5 Group velocity (Chapter 5)







group velocity
\(v_g=d\omega/dk=c/N_g\)


group index
\(N_g=n-\lambda\,dn/d\lambda\)


beat of two waves
\(E=2E_0\cos(\delta\omega t-\delta kz)\cos(\omega t-kz)\)


group delay
\(\tau_g=LN_g/c\)


material dispersion
\(D=-\dfrac{\lambda}{c}\dfrac{d^2n}{d\lambda^2}\)

title: Appendix B — Formula sheet
text:
B.6 Snell’s law and TIR (Chapter 6)







reflection
\(\theta_r=\theta_i\)


Snell
\(n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t\)


critical angle
\(\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1\) (\(n_1>n_2\))


lateral displacement
\(d=L\sin\theta_i\left[1-\dfrac{\cos\theta_i}{\sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta_i}}\right]\)


numerical aperture
\(\mathrm{NA}=n_0\sin\theta_a=\sqrt{n_1^2-n_2^2}\)


Fermat
the actual path makes the travel time stationary

title: Appendix B — Formula sheet
text:
B.7 Fresnel equations (Chapter 7)







\(r_\perp\)
\(\dfrac{\cos\theta_i-\sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta_i}}{\cos\theta_i+\sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta_i}}\), \(\ n=n_2/n_1\)


\(r_\parallel\)
\(\dfrac{\sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta_i}-n^2\cos\theta_i}{\sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta_i}+n^2\cos\theta_i}\)


\(t\) relations
\(t_\perp=1+r_\perp\), \(\ r_\parallel+nt_\parallel=1\)


normal incidence
\(R=\left(\dfrac{n_1-n_2}{n_1+n_2}\right)^2\) (glass: 4 %)


Brewster
\(\tan\theta_p=n_2/n_1\) (\(r_\parallel=0\))


TIR phase ⊥
\(\tan(\phi_\perp/2)=\sqrt{\sin^2\theta_i-n^2}/\cos\theta_i\)


TIR phase ∥
\(\tan(\phi_\parallel/2+\pi/2)=\sqrt{\sin^2\theta_i-n^2}/(n^2\cos\theta_i)\)


evanescent decay
\(\alpha_2=\dfrac{2\pi n_2}{\lambda}\sqrt{\dfrac{n_1^2}{n_2^2}\sin^2\theta_i-1}\), \(\ \delta=1/\alpha_2\)


Goos–Hänchen
\(\Delta z\approx2\delta\tan\theta_i\)


transmittance
\(T=\dfrac{n_2\cos\theta_t}{n_1\cos\theta_i}\lvert t\rvert^2=1-R\)

title: Appendix B — Formula sheet
text:
B.8 Thin films (Chapter 8)







round-trip phase
\(\phi=2\cdot\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}n_2d\)


film reflection
\(r=\dfrac{r_{12}+r_{23}e^{-j\phi}}{1+r_{12}r_{23}e^{-j\phi}}\)


AR coating
\(d=m\dfrac{\lambda}{4n_2}\) (\(m\) odd), \(\ n_2=\sqrt{n_1n_3}\)


\(R_\text{min}\) (\(n_1<n_2<n_3\))
\(\left(\dfrac{n_1n_3-n_2^2}{n_1n_3+n_2^2}\right)^2\) at \(\phi=\) odd \(\pi\)


\(R_\text{max}\) (\(n_1<n_2<n_3\))
\(\left(\dfrac{n_3-n_1}{n_3+n_1}\right)^2\) at \(\phi=\) even \(\pi\)


incoherent plate
\(T=(1-R)/(1+R)\)

title: Appendix B — Formula sheet
text:
B.9 Coherence and interference (Chapter 9, Chapter 10)



coherence time
\(\Delta t\approx1/\Delta\nu\)


coherence length
\(l_c=c\Delta t=\lambda^2/\Delta\lambda\)


Gaussian pulse
\(\Delta t\,\Delta\nu\approx0.44\) (FWHM)


two-beam interference
\(I=I_1+I_2+2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\delta\)


phase difference
\(\delta=k(r_2-r_1)+(\phi_2-\phi_1)\)


visibility
\(V=\dfrac{2\sqrt{I_1I_2}}{I_1+I_2}\)


Mach–Zehnder
\(I\propto\cos^2(\Phi/2)\); quadrature at \(\Phi=\pi/2\)


unbalanced MZI
\(\mathrm{FSR}=\lambda^2/(N_g\Delta L)\)


etalon rings
\(2nL\cos\theta=m\lambda\)

title: Appendix B — Formula sheet
text:
B.10 Bragg mirrors (Chapter 11)







Bragg condition
\(n_1d_1+n_2d_2=m\lambda/2\)


quarter-wave stack
\(d_1=\lambda/4n_1\), \(\ d_2=\lambda/4n_2\)


peak reflectance
\(R_N=\left[\dfrac{n_0n_2^{2N}-n_3n_1^{2N}}{n_0n_2^{2N}+n_3n_1^{2N}}\right]^2\)


stop band
\(\Delta\lambda\approx\dfrac{4\lambda_0}{\pi}\arcsin\dfrac{n_1-n_2}{n_1+n_2}\)


penetration depth
\(L_\text{pen}=-\tfrac12\,d\phi/dk\approx\lambda/(4\Delta n)\)


1D band structure
\(\cos K\Lambda=\cos k_1d_1\cos k_2d_2-\tfrac12\left(\tfrac{n_1}{n_2}+\tfrac{n_2}{n_1}\right)\sin k_1d_1\sin k_2d_2\)

title: Appendix B — Formula sheet
text:
B.11 Fabry–Perot (Chapter 12)







modes
\(m\lambda_m/2=nL\), \(\ \nu_m=mc/(2nL)\)


free spectral range
\(\nu_f=c/(2nL)\), \(\ \Delta\lambda=\lambda^2/(2nL)\)


finesse
\(\mathcal F=\dfrac{\pi\sqrt R}{1-R}\)


linewidth
\(\delta\nu_m=\nu_f/\mathcal F\)


quality factor
\(Q=\nu_m/\delta\nu_m=m\mathcal F\)


Airy transmission
\(T=\dfrac{(1-R)^2}{(1-R)^2+4R\sin^2(2\pi nL/\lambda)}\)

title: Appendix B — Formula sheet
text:
B.12 Diffraction and scattering (Chapter 13, Chapter 14)







Fraunhofer regime
\(z\gg D\) and \(z\gg\pi D^2/\lambda\)


single slit
\(I=I_0\,\mathrm{sinc}^2\beta\), \(\ \beta=\pi a\sin\theta/\lambda\); zeros \(\sin\theta=m\lambda/a\)


circular aperture
\(I=I_0[2J_1(\gamma)/\gamma]^2\), \(\ \gamma=\tfrac12kD\sin\theta\)


Rayleigh criterion
\(\sin\Delta\theta_\text{min}=1.22\lambda/D\)


grating
\(d(\sin\theta_m-\sin\theta_i)=m\lambda\)


blaze
\(2\gamma=\theta_m-\theta_i\)


resolving power
\(\lambda/\Delta\lambda=mN\)


Rayleigh scattering
\(\alpha_R\propto\lambda^{-4}\), pattern \(\propto1+\cos^2\theta\)


Brillouin shift
\(\nu_B=2nv_a/\lambda\)
